Designing a phenology study around cloud

Source: vignettes/phenology.Rmd
phenology.Rmd

The question

You want land-surface phenology from optical imagery. Before committing, you want to know whether the site will yield a defensible green-up date, and if not, what would change that.

Mean cloud cover cannot answer this. Two sites with identical 60% annual cloud can differ by a factor of three in retrieval error, depending on when the cloud falls and how it clusters.

Step 1: how many observations, and when 

dates <- seq(as.Date("2023-01-01"), as.Date("2023-12-31"), by = "5 days")
site <- cl_simulate_series(dates, p_cloud = 0.62, persistence = 0.4, seed = 11)
obs <- cl_obs(cell = 1, date = site$date, cloud_fraction = site$cloud_fraction,
              sensor = "sentinel-2-msi")

cl_stats_wide(cl_gaps(obs, threshold = 0.2, critical = 21))
#>   cell period         sensor max_gap_days mean_gap_days n_clear_obs
#> 1    1   2023 sentinel-2-msi           95            26          13

The maximum gap matters more than the count. A 40-day gap that happens to straddle green-up removes the transition entirely, and no amount of data later in the season recovers it.

Step 2: translate into days of error 

p <- cl_pheno_power(dates, cloud_fraction = site$cloud_fraction,
                    n_sim = 300, seed = 2)
p$summary[, c("n_usable_median", "sos_mae", "sos_iqr", "sos_bias",
              "failure_rate")]
#>   n_usable_median sos_mae sos_iqr sos_bias failure_rate
#> 1              34     2.3     4.7      0.2   0.04333333

Read the failure rate first. It is the fraction of years in which the double-logistic fit does not converge at all. A study that fails to produce an estimate is a different problem from one that produces a biased estimate, and the two get confused when only mean error is reported.

Step 3: how sensitive is this to clustering? 

grid <- expand.grid(cloud = c(0.4, 0.6, 0.8), rho = c(0, 0.35, 0.7))
res <- do.call(rbind, Map(function(cl, rho) {
  s <- cl_pheno_power(dates, cloud_fraction = cl, persistence = rho,
                      n_sim = 250, seed = 5)$summary
  data.frame(cloud = cl, rho = rho, usable = s$n_usable_median,
             sos_mae = s$sos_mae, failure = round(s$failure_rate, 3))
}, grid$cloud, grid$rho))
res
#>   cloud  rho usable sos_mae failure
#> 1   0.4 0.00   43.0    0.80   0.000
#> 2   0.6 0.00   29.0    1.10   0.020
#> 3   0.8 0.00   14.0    2.20   0.220
#> 4   0.4 0.35   43.0    1.00   0.008
#> 5   0.6 0.35   28.5    1.30   0.036
#> 6   0.8 0.35   14.0    3.35   0.296
#> 7   0.4 0.70   43.5    0.90   0.044
#> 8   0.6 0.70   28.0    1.65   0.136
#> 9   0.8 0.70   13.0    7.20   0.412

Along any row of constant cloud, the number of usable observations barely moves, but the failure rate climbs with rho. Clustering does not remove observations; it removes them from where they matter. Any feasibility assessment that assumes independent cloud loss will be optimistic, and the more so the more clustered the local climate.

Step 4: would adding a sensor fix it? 

sy <- cl_synergy(c("landsat-8-9-oli", "sentinel-2-msi"),
                 "2015-01-01", "2025-12-31")
sy[sy$period == "2025", c("sensor", "n_platforms", "combined_obs",
                          "effective_revisit_days")]
#>             sensor n_platforms combined_obs effective_revisit_days
#> 33        COMBINED           5      155.125               2.354553
#> 21 landsat-8-9-oli           2       45.625               8.005479
#> 22  sentinel-2-msi           3      109.500               3.335616

Adding Landsat to Sentinel-2 shortens effective revisit substantially. Whether that converts into usable observations depends on whether the two constellations are clouded at the same times, which they largely are — so the gain is real but smaller than the revisit numbers alone suggest. Verify with the actual archive rather than assuming.

Step 5: state the design explicitly 

cl_feasibility(p_clear = 0.38, n_acquisitions = 73, n_required = 15,
               window_days = 365, max_gap = 30)
#> $expected_obs
#> [1] 27.74
#> 
#> $p_sufficient
#> [1] 0.9995714
#> 
#> $p_gap_ok
#> [1] 0.189
#> 
#> $n_sim
#> [1] 2000

What to report in a paper

State the acquisition count, the maximum gap, and the simulated retrieval error with its failure rate, for each site or stratum. Reporting mean cloud cover alone leaves reviewers unable to judge whether the phenological conclusions are supportable, and leaves you unable to explain why one site behaved differently from another.

A caveat worth carrying: everything above uses tier-A cloud fractions, which are scene averages. They give an upper bound on usable observations. Recomputing with tier = "qa" on the actual quality layers will lower these numbers, and the gap between the two is itself informative.
